idiom_name: Data.define nodes + Array path; Data#with rebuilds the parent
implementation_notes: Ruby's value-object primitive is Data (Data.define, Ruby 3.2+): instances have no member writers, and #with returns a new instance with changed members - which is exactly the rebuild-the-parent step - so a zipper is a Data-defined Node, a Data-defined Loc holding the focus plus an Array of [parent, index] frames, and one method per verb. What replaces the classic structure is #with plus frozen arrays; what stays hand-written is the context, and because #with and #dup are shallow copies, children must be frozen (or rebuilt from fresh arrays) or the previous version mutates through the shared array. Mutable class graphs (Nokogiri-style nodes with parent links) remain the right choice for in-place document editing.
code_sketch:
Node = Data.define(:text, :kids)      # no writers; #with returns an updated copy
Loc  = Data.define(:focus, :path)     # path: [[parent, index], ...] from focus to root

def up(loc)                            # rebuild the parent once
  parent, index = loc.path.last
  kids = parent.kids.dup
  kids[index] = loc.focus
  Loc.new(focus: parent.with(kids: kids.freeze), path: loc.path[0..-2])
end
# Node.new(text: "a", kids: [].freeze); up(loc).focus # => the rebuilt parent
pitfalls: Data#with and #dup are shallow: an unfrozen Array field is shared with the copy, so mutating it changes the original - freeze child arrays explicitly.
Data instances are not deeply frozen: freeze/frozen? are per-object, so every level of an update must be rebuilt for the guarantee to hold.
Struct is the older primitive and still has member writers and mutable members; using it for the tree reintroduces the mutation the pattern removes.
Hash/Array are reference types: storing the path as a shared array that is later mutated in place corrupts locations held elsewhere.
